1.pericope_label: The fire came down from heaven, and the glory of the Lord filled the house: the people bow upon the pavement

schools.summary: Gill wonders whether a second distinct fire is meant, since this one seems to descend upon the house and may denote a bright shining light, and explains that the priests had gone in to carry the ark and, unable to stand and minister, came out and could not re-enter.

Henry fixes on the timing, that the fire fell upon the praying and not upon the killing of the sacrifices, as it had for Moses, Gideon, David and Elijah, and reads the sign double: God glorious in himself, a consuming fire breaking from the thick darkness, and gracious to Israel, since the fire that might justly have consumed the people fastened on the sacrifice offered in their stead.

Clarke sets the two signs in sequence, the cloud having come down before and the fire now consuming the offering, so that both house and sacrifices are shown accepted; Wesley takes the fire for the token of acceptance, orders the cloud as descending upon the house and then entering it, and reads the prostration as dread, submission and a sense of unworthiness together.

Ellicott marks the point where the two accounts diverge and defends the chronicler against the charge of invention, insists the glory is a manifestation distinct from the fire and that two separate appearances are intended, and glosses the pavement from the Greek and the versions; Delitzsch reports the critical charge that the narrative is a later unhistorical embellishment, absent from Kings where a speech of Solomon stands instead.

debates.question: Did the chronicler invent the fire from heaven?

sides.position: no: there is no objective ground for the supposition, he must have found it in one of his sources, and it is gratuitous to think him more partial to miracle than the older writer
modern criticism has rejected the narrative as a later unhistorical embellishment, since Kings has a speech of Solomon in its place

debates.question: How many manifestations are there, and of what?

sides.position: the glory is distinct from the fire, and the writer records two separate appearances of the glory, one before and one after the prayer
the second may itself be a distinct fire, since it seems to come down upon the house
one cloud, which came down upon the house and then entered it, seen within by the priests and without by the people

outliers: Henry alone presses the fire as a figure both of the suffering of Christ, the sacrifice consumed that others might escape, and of the sanctification of the Spirit, which burns up the lusts that must be sacrificed.
Ellicott alone observes that hardly anything in the whole section, apart from the refrain about mercy enduring for ever, can be called characteristic of the chronicler’s own style.
themes: fire falling on a prayer rather than on a victim
a glory counted twice
priests unable to re-enter their own house
a people flat on a tesselated floor

4.pericope_label: Then the king and all the people offered sacrifices before the Lord: the priests at their posts, and an altar too small

schools.summary: Gill divides the priestly work between those offering sacrifices and those blowing trumpets, and turns the dedication of the altar into a comparative note, that the heathen imitated the practice with ashes and water as Pausanias relates and held feasts at the dedication of their temples, in which they have themselves been imitated by Christians.

Clarke leaves open whether the people or the priests killed the victims, and makes the twenty-two thousand oxen the sum of all offered through both weeks; Wesley traces the music to its origin in David, who composed the psalms, appointed the Levites to sing them and joined instruments to their voices.

Ellicott keeps to the Hebrew and the parallels, noting the words about peace offerings that seem to have dropped out, that the sixth verse is the chronicler’s own addition in his usual fashion of stressing the ritual and its choral side, and that the English rightly makes the Levites David’s ministers of praise against the Greek; Delitzsch calls the dedication concluded by a great thank-offering and treats the seventh verse as a supplementary remark to be read as a pluperfect.

sides.position: either the people presented them to the priests, who slew them and sprinkled the blood, or the people slew them and presented the blood and fat

debates.question: What does the closing phrase of the sixth verse mean?

sides.position: the Greek takes the word substantively, as though it meant in David’s psalmody, perhaps with the great hallel in view
the English gives the true sense, that the Levites were David’s ministers of praise

outliers: Gill alone traces a line from the dedication of this altar through the pagan dedications Pausanias describes to the English country feasts, which he says were first kept at the dedication of churches to one saint or another.
Clarke alone reads the twenty-two thousand oxen as a cumulative total for both festivals rather than a single day’s offering.
themes: a question of who wielded the knife
a verse the chronicler added for the music
an altar that could not hold the offerings
a dedication the heathen copied

8.pericope_label: And Solomon kept the feast seven days: fourteen days reckoned, and the people sent away glad

schools.summary: Gill observes only that from this point the narrative runs with the older account.

Clarke takes the northern limit of the gathering from the Targum, from the entrance of Antioch to the Nile of Egypt, harmonises the eighth day of Kings with the twenty-third here by way of Jarchi, and passes on the Targum’s expansion of the dismissal, where the people go home glad for David, for Solomon and for Israel in turn.

Ellicott identifies the feast as Tabernacles kept its legal seven days from the fifteenth of the month, explains the obscure fourteen days of Kings as an extraordinary inauguration week followed by Tabernacles in course, and removes the discrepancy over the day of dismissal by noting that the twenty-third begins with the evening of the twenty-second; Delitzsch marks the passage as the close of the dedication proper.

debates.question: How are the eighth day of Kings and the twenty-third day here reconciled?

sides.position: no discrepancy exists, since the twenty-third begins with the evening of the twenty-second
leave was given on the eighth day and many returned then, the remainder being dismissed on the ninth, which is the twenty-third once the fourteen days of the two feasts are reckoned in

debates.question: What are the seven days and seven days of Kings?

sides.position: an extraordinary festival for the inauguration of the house, the eighth to the fourteenth of Ethanim, followed by the seven legal days of Tabernacles, as the Syriac spells out

outliers: Clarke alone preserves the Targum’s threefold expansion of the dismissal, in which the doors of the sanctuary stood open for David’s sake, the prayer was heard for Solomon’s, and the heavenly fire descended for Israel’s.
Ellicott alone notes that the mention of Solomon beside David is the chronicler’s addition, consistent with his habit of connecting all Solomon’s success with the promise made to David.
themes: a feast with a legal length and an added week
a torrent rather than a river
two numberings of one dismissal
a people glad for three reasons

12.pericope_label: The Lord appeared to Solomon by night: if my people shall humble themselves and pray, then will I heal their land

schools.summary: Gill observes that everything from here to the end runs with the older book except the verses answering Solomon’s particular requests about famine and pestilence, which are given as a specimen and as encouragement to expect the same treatment in every other case he had named.

Henry separates the two answers, the fire having shown the prayer accepted while a prayer may be accepted and yet not answered in the letter of it, and reads the conditions as a national doctrine: God expects a people who have dishonoured his name by their iniquity to honour it by accepting the punishment of their iniquity, and all their humbling and praying will not do unless they turn from their wicked ways.

Clarke notes the second manifestation and supplies the Targum throughout, where it is the Word of the Lord that appears, the pestilence is the angel of death, and the opened eyes become a pleasure in the sight of the Word.

Ellicott observes that the night is only implied in the older text, that house of sacrifice occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament, and that the added section must by its style have belonged to an original narrative both writers drew on; he traces each clause of the condition to its parallel and identifies the locust as a winged edible species. Delitzsch grants that the contents and order of thought agree in the two accounts and locates the differences in the individual expressions.

debates.question: Where did the added section come from?

sides.position: from an original narrative used by both writers, as the style shows, rather than from a later hand
the two accounts agree in contents and in the order of the thoughts, differing only in individual expressions
the added verses are a specimen answer to Solomon’s particular requests, given as encouragement for the rest

debates.question: What are the locusts that devour the land?

sides.position: a winged and edible species, where the chapter before had named two other kinds
perhaps enemies are meant, as greedy as locusts and laying all waste

outliers: Henry alone states the demand at its sharpest, that a people who have dishonoured God’s name by their iniquity should honour it by accepting the punishment of their iniquity.
Ellicott alone notes that the phrase house of sacrifice occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament.
Clarke alone preserves the Targum’s substitution of the Word of the Lord for the Lord himself in the night appearance.
themes: a second answer after the fire
a house of sacrifice and a house of prayer
humbling, praying, seeking and turning
a land healed as well as forgiven

17.pericope_label: And as for thee, if thou wilt walk before me: the condition for the throne, and the house laid in heaps

schools.summary: Clarke reads the section as fulfilled history: the promise failed because the condition failed, the plucking up by the roots has left the nation neither root nor branch, and the ruin is astonishing because no people were ever so highly favoured or so signally punished; while they cleaved to God no enemy could touch them, and once they forsook him the weakest of their foes reduced them to bondage.

Ellicott works the text throughout: the omitted words of the covenant formula and the possible misreading behind them, the reminiscence of Micah substituted where the word throne had dropped out, the lost and your children, the two places where the chronicler softens the severity of Kings, and the argument that this house which is high was originally this house shall become ruinous heaps.

debates.question: What did the house that is high originally say?

sides.position: that it shall become ruinous heaps, the Hebrew for heaps and for high differing very little; the Syriac and Arabic read laid waste in both books and the Targum of Kings combines the two, and the mistake is as old as the Greek
the received reading stands, and the astonishment it describes has been literally fulfilled

debates.question: Why was the promise of a perpetual throne not kept?

sides.position: because the condition was not kept: they forsook God, and he cut them off, and the throne with them

outliers: Ellicott alone identifies two places where the chronicler eases the harsher language of Kings, which would cut off Israel from the face of the land and let Israel become a byword.

Clarke alone generalises the warning into a law of the national history, that Israel resisted its enemies by no prowess or tactics of its own but by divine power alone, destitute of which they were even worse than other men.
themes: a covenant verb with its noun missing
children fallen out of a threat
a high house or a heap of ruins
a hiss the older text keeps
